CausalChain: Gut dysbiosis -> Increased production of microbiota-derived metabolites -> Chronic inflammatory cytokine milieu (e.g., IL-6, IL-17) -> Upregulation of CD39/CD73 on MDSCs -> Enhanced conversion of extracellular ATP to immunosuppressive adenosine -> Augmented T-cell suppression and immune evasion -> Reduced efficacy of checkpoint inhibitors
Hypothesis: In colorectal cancer, gut microbiota‐derived metabolites reprogram MDSCs to overexpress adenosine‐generating enzymes (CD39 and CD73), thereby augmenting adenosine-mediated immunosuppression and contributing to resistance to immunotherapy. Targeting this microbiota–MDSC–adenosine axis may improve patient responses to checkpoint inhibition.
Abstract: Recent advances in understanding the multifaceted roles of myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in cancer immunosuppression have highlighted not only their direct mechanisms of immune evasion but also the influence of the tumor microenvironment and systemic factors on their function. Here, we propose that in colorectal cancer (CRC), the gut microbiota–derived metabolites play a pivotal role in modulating the immunosuppressive activity of MDSCs through the upregulation of adenosine‐generating enzymes. Specifically, microbiota-induced chronic inflammation and altered cytokine profiles may enhance the expression of CD39 and CD73 on MDSCs. This metabolic reprogramming amplifies local adenosine production, thereby fostering a stronger immunosuppressive milieu and contributing to resistance against checkpoint inhibitor therapies. Targeting this axis, either by modulating gut microbial composition or by directly inhibiting the adenosinergic pathway in MDSCs, represents a novel and testable therapeutic strategy to reverse MDSC-mediated immunosuppression in CRC.
